\opt{A}{$\beta=3\sqrt{14}\times10^8$}
\opt{B}{b = 2}
\opt{C}{Average energy density of wave is $6.5\times10^{-6}\varepsilon_0$ in SI unit.}
\opt{D}{Amplitude of magnetic field is $1.2\times10^{-11}$ T.}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{$B_x=-2\times10^{-7}\sin\left[2\pi\left(5\times10^{14}t-\dfrac{10^7}{3}z\right)\right]$ Wb$m^{-2}$}
\opt{B}{$B_y=2\times10^{-7}\sin\left[2\pi\left(5\times10^{14}t-\dfrac{10^7}{3}z\right)\right]$ Wb$m^{-2}$}
\opt{C}{The wave is polarized in the xy-plane with polarization angle $\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac12\right)$ with respect to the x-axis.}
\opt{D}{The refractive index of the medium is 1.5.}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

\begin{bankq}[id=SII30-P1-PHY-S1-Q03, source={Score-II - Test 30 (27 Mar 2024)}, paper=1, qno=3, type=single, subtopic={Properties}, answer={C}, answer_src=key, difficulty=1, diff_parts={K1 S1 I0 C0 F0}, diff_note={concepts: match Maxwell equations with their names | steps: identify Ampere Maxwell, Gauss laws and Faraday law; match}]
Match List I with List II
\par\nobreak
\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{|c|p{3.3cm}|c|p{1.9cm}|}\hline
 & \multicolumn{1}{c|}{\textbf{List I}} & & \multicolumn{1}{c|}{\textbf{List II}}\\\hline
A. & $\displaystyle\oint\vec B\cdot\vec{dl}=\mu_0i_c+\mu_0\varepsilon_0\dfrac{d\phi_E}{dt}$ & I. & Gauss' law for electricity\\\hline

\end{tabular}

\opt{B}{A-II, B-III, C-I, D-IV}

\opt{D}{A-I, B-II, C-III, D-IV}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

\begin{bankpassage}[id=SA39-P1-PHY-S3-G3-4, source={Score Advanced - Test 39 (20 Apr 2025)}, questions={3-4}]
The blue of the sky and the red of the sunset are due to a phenomenon called ``scattering''. When sunlight passes through the earth's atmosphere, much of the light is picked up by the air molecules and given out again in some other direction. Experiments show, in agreement with the theory of scattering, that the shortest waves are scattered more readily then longer waves. To more specific, the scattering is inversely proportional to the fourth power of the wavelength.\par
scattering $\propto\dfrac1{\lambda^4}$\par
For every ten violet wave ($\lambda$ = 4 $\times$ 10$^{-7}$ m) scattered from a beam, there is only one red wave ($\lambda$ = 7 $\times$ 10$^{-7}$ m). Scattering of different colours will be in the ratio as given below :\par
{\footnotesize\setlength{\tabcolsep}{4pt}\noindent\begin{tabular}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline
Violet & Blue & Green & Yellow & Orange & Red \\ \hline
10 & 6 & 3 & 2.5 & 2 & 1 \\ \hline
\end{tabular}}\par
\end{bankpassage}

Two plane electromagnetic waves with the same amplitude E$_0$ and frequency $\omega$ travel in opposite directions along the z-axis, creating a standing wave. The electric field vectors of these waves are given by :\par
$\vec{\mathrm E}_1$(z, t) = E$_0$ cos(kz $-$ $\omega$t)$\hat{\mathrm i}$, $\vec{\mathrm E}_2$(z, t) = E$_0$ cos(kz + $\omega$t + $\phi$)$\hat{\mathrm i}$\par
The superposition of these two waves forms a standing wave. Select the correct statements.
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{When $\phi=\dfrac\pi2$, the resulting wave is elliptically polarized and the polarization changes with position along the z-axis.}
\opt{B}{If $\phi=\pi$, the resulting wave is linearly polarized along a fixed direction in the xy-plane.}
\opt{C}{The magnetic field vector of the resulting wave oscillates perpendicular to the plane of polarization at each point.}
\opt{D}{For $\phi=\pi$, nodes of the electric field occur at positions z = $\dfrac{\mathrm n\pi}{\mathrm k}$, where n is an integer.}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
